articles.title: Solheim Cup: History suggests Europe v US will be another thriller at Bernardus Golf Club
articles.summary: With no more than one point separating the teams at the past three Solheim Cups played in Europe there is every reason to expect that this week's contest will be just as exciting, writes Iain Carter.
articles.body:
Recent history suggests this week's Solheim Cup will be another epic clash to follow hot on the heels of Great Britain and Ireland's dramatic victory over the United States in the Walker Cup.

The extraordinary climax at Lahinch last Sunday, where GB&I won with the last putt of the match, evoked memories of the past three Solheim Cups staged in Europe.

Three years ago in Spain the contest ended in a dramatic 14-14 tie to allow a delirious European team to hold on to the trophy, having initially wrestled it from American hands with a single-point victory at Gleneagles in 2019.

Then it was Suzann Pettersen's gut wrenching and ultimately successful putt on the final green at the Scottish course that decided the outcome.

And the previous Solheim Cup held on continental soil was a 2015 single point away win that capped an astonishing comeback by the United States in Germany.

So the past three matches in Europe have had no more than a point in them and the home team and the US are tied on aggregate at 42 points apiece.

"I think it just shows how important each game is," said British number one Lottie Woad, who makes her debut for Europe this week.

"Even if you're a couple down early, you can get it back and even just getting a half point could be vital. So I think you've just got to have that mentality that any half point or point helps."

Woad's compatriot and potential partner Charley Hull believes it can be tougher playing at home. "We get big crowds in both places, but obviously, it's a little more pressure over here when it's a home Solheim Cup," she said.

"You've just got to deal with it, just stay focused, and be in the zone."

Woad is among four rookies in the European team joining fellow Englishwoman Mimi Rhodes, France's Nastasia Nadaud and the big hitting Spaniard Julia Lopez Ramirez.

"I can't wait for them to tee it up," said European captain Anna Nordqvist. "It's always easy to try to describe to the rookies what it's like playing in the Solheim, but it's something that you need to experience.

"And you have to get your own feel for it. But I can't wait for them to feel what it's like stepping up on that first tee."

Players prepare for the intimidation of packed crowds in a huge grandstand around three sides of the opening tee, but of more significance will be the play as matches reach their climax down the closing stretch of holes.

And that will be amplified further if it is again close in the closing singles matches on Sunday. "Obviously it's elevated," said 2025 US Open winner Maja Stark.

"But you're still just playing golf and you're trying to do your best and you're trying to beat one person. There's not much more you can do.

"You can't rely on team-mates on Sunday afternoon. You have got to go back and remember what's important for me now."

The three-day contest starts on Friday with four foursomes - alternate shot - matches, with four fourball matches to follow. That format is replicated on Saturday before the 12 singles matches on Sunday.

American captain Angela Stanford is bullish about her line-up's ability to handle the unique pressure of the Solheim Cup. "I think they're very mentally tough," she said.

"They don't let things bother them. They let things kind of roll off their back if something doesn't go the way they planned and they seem really focused."

Ironically none of the 24 players are bringing stellar individual form into this match, not even Nelly Korda, the world number one who claimed her fourth title of the year by winning the US Women's Open in June.

Korda has had only two top-10s since that major triumph at the start of the summer and finished in a lowly share of 50th place at the recent FM Championship.

Since Korda's US Open victory there have been no LPGA wins for any of the Solheim players.

For Europe only Celine Boutier and Woad have claimed titles this season and American Lauren Coughlin is the sole other tour winner in 2026 on show.

But that backdrop will be forgotten when it comes to head-to-head matchplay. As the Walker Cup showed it goes to a rarified level when put into the team environment.

"You can lose or win any match regardless of rankings or how you're playing at the moment," said Linn Grant, Stark's Swedish compatriot who has missed the cut in five of her past six events.

"When everyone shows up on Friday, you're just going to bring your best game.

"It's so different playing matchplay in this setting. It's kind of like just everyone's best game just shows up normally which makes it a lot more fun to play as well."

They are competing on a testing course at Bernardus Golf near Hertogenbosch in the Netherlands, which hosted the Dutch Open on the DP World Tour from 2021-23. It has a Surrey heathland feel, that can play like a seaside links in certain areas.

But that fast running aspect has been compromised by the storms that lashed the layout on Wednesday. "I think it's a great course for matchplay," said Stark.

"There are a lot of bunkers that you don't really want to be in. You can have a lot of really long irons into par-four holes as well."

The par threes are also likely to generate plenty of drama, especially the 15th where matches will reach a crucial stage. "It is my favourite hole both visually and strategically," says Bernardus club professional Roel Verdonschot.

"It is built for drama. Players must decide whether to take the risk and attack the pin for a short birdie opportunity or play towards the middle of the green and accept a longer putt.

"The tee is sheltered, so the wind can be difficult to feel, even though it is still influencing the shot."

And any match that goes the distance will involve an exceptionally tough 389-yard par-four closing hole. There is water from the left of the tee, while bunkers await players attempting to play safely towards the right.

And the green is tiny with a deep run-off to the left and water to the right. "The 18th is the most difficult playing hole at Bernardus," said Verdonschot.

"You face a tee shot that you cannot afford to miss left, but you do not want to miss right either. If a close match reaches the 18th, there is a very good chance of drama."

Which is completely in keeping with Solheim Cup matches, especially those staged in Europe.

articles.title: What Will the 2026 Dolphins Passing Game Look Like? Let’s Ask the 2022–2023 Packers
articles.summary: Packers’ philosophy gives insight into how Dolphins receiver’s room may develop.
articles.body:
The Packers built a passing game without a WR1 — and the Dolphins might do the same.

The Dolphins are heading into 2026 with one of the youngest receiver rooms in the league, with three rookies and a second‑year player expected to play real snaps – all catching passes from an unproven, first‑time starting quarterback. That might sound terrifying in the short term, but we actually have a modern template for how this can work: The Packers from 2022–2023, who rebuilt their pass‑catcher group while transitioning to Jordan Love .

The parallels are striking: A young quarterback stepping into a bigger role, a receiver room built almost entirely from scratch and a front office willing to bet on development. Jon‑Eric Sullivan helped architect Green Bay 's youth movement, drafting Christian Watson , Romeo Doubs , Jayden Reed , and Dontayvion Wicks in a two-year span, and now he's trying to build the same long‑term payoff in Green Bay South.

Even early in the youth movement, Green Bay's passing game was solid – which is perhaps to be expected when you have a first‑ballot Hall of Famer behind center. In 2022, Aaron Rodgers ' final season with the Packers, the team finished with 3,890 passing yards and 26 passing touchdowns. Fifteen different players caught passes, and eight of them topped 200 receiving yards. Among the rookies, Christian Watson finished second on the team with 611 yards and 7 touchdowns, while Romeo Doubs added 425 yards and 3 scores.

In 2023, with Jordan Love taking over, the passing numbers improved. Love threw for 4,159 yards and 32 touchdowns, and once again the ball was spread widely: sixteen players caught passes, and nine of them reached 200+ receiving yards. Reed, Doubs, Wicks, and Watson combined for roughly 2,500 yards and 25 touchdowns, but none eclipsed 800 yards – a sign that the Packers built the room around depth. (Incidentally, the trend continued beyond these transitional years. Reed and Doubs led the team in 2024 and 2025 with 857 yards and 724 yards, respectively, and six touchdowns apiece.)

This isn't apples to apples – Miami's offense will look different. For one, the attack will likely run through De'Von Achane, who Jeff Hafley joked would get the ball 40–45 times per game . And Malik Willis brings a running element that Jordan Love didn't, which will change how defenses play Miami.

But when Willis does throw, the distribution may look a lot like Green Bay's. The Dolphins have six receivers on their 53‑man roster, plus Achane, pass‑catching tight end Greg Dulcich , and several other skill players who can handle targets. The Packers' young receivers made an impact right away – Reed led the team in yards as a rookie – but at no point did they produce a traditional WR1 with 1,000 yards and double‑digit touchdowns. Miami's passing game may follow the same pattern, with broad distribution, steady growth and no single player dominating the stat sheet.

As much as we all might love a breakout 1,200‑yard receiver in Miami this season to replace the Cheetah and the Penguin, that might be setting us up for disappointment. But if you can live with a deep and versatile group that gets better as the year goes on – the Packers showed that's absolutely possible. And with Jon‑Eric Sullivan now running Miami's roster, it's no coincidence the Dolphins are trying to build something similar.

articles.title: Solheim Cup: tres días de juego y un recuerdo para toda la vida
articles.standfirst: Las golfistas españolas que jugaron la gran competición comparten sus experiencias antes de una edición que contempla el debut de Julia López junto a la eterna Carlota Ciganda
articles.summary: Las golfistas españolas que jugaron la gran competición comparten sus experiencias antes de una edición que contempla el debut de Julia López junto a la eterna Carlota Ciganda
articles.body: Hay torneos que se ganan. La Solheim Cup, además, se vive. Las siete españolas que han disputado el torneo bienal entre Europa y Estados Unidos, y que comienza este viernes en el Bernardus Golf de Países Bajos, guarda recuerdos que van más allá de un resultado: nervios imposibles, bromas en el vestuario, consejos de leyendas, padres al borde del infarto y compañeras que acabaron siendo amigas para siempre. Ahora, mientras Julia López se prepara para estrenarse, ellas recuerdan por qué esta competición no se parece a ninguna otra. No importa si eres Raquel Carriedo en Escocia en el año 2000, Paula Martí dos años después en Minnesota, Ana Belén Sánchez en Suecia, Azahara Muñoz en Irlanda, Tania Elósegui en Illinois, Carlota Ciganda y Beatriz Recari en Colorado o Julia López en Holanda este fin de semana. Todas llegaron al tee del 1 pensando exactamente lo mismo. "¿Qué hago yo aquí?". Lo reconoce Carriedo, la que abrió las puertas. Cuando se clasificó para la Solheim Cup de Loch Lomond, aún no había ganado un torneo profesional. Había logrado nueve segundos puestos, pero seguía sintiéndose pequeña al entrar en un vestuario lleno de estrellas. "Me sentía rara, inferior, y eso mentalmente me influía”. Hasta que apareció Laura Davies, una de las grandes leyendas del golf europeo, que supo perfectamente cómo se sentía la debutante española y ha ejercido de “madrina” de muchas de ellas. Aquella primera Solheim fue cualquier cosa menos cómoda: lluvia, frío, suspensiones de juego, madrugones para recuperar hoyos y una tensión constante. "Fue un recuerdo bonito, pero durísimo. Terminaba reventada. Lo recuerdo agotador. Aunque ganamos, tengo muchos mejores recuerdos de la siguiente en Minnesota, y eso que ahí perdimos”, donde vivió uno de esos momentos que no se olvidan. Jugaba junto a Karine Icher contra Christie Kerr y Rosie Jones, las estrellas de la competición. "Estábamos jugando increíble y, en mitad de la vuelta, Kerr se acercó y nos dijo: 'Ya podéis hacer malabarismos… que hoy no os vamos a ganar’”. Aunque el punto de inflexión fue aquella primera Solheim tras la cual llegaron las victorias, los patrocinios, el caddie profesional, “La Solheim del 2000 me cambió la vida”. Dos años después llegó Martí con la misma sensación. La capitana Dale Reid le comunicó una noticia difícil de creer. "Hay dos jugadoras que quieren jugar contigo: Annika Sörenstam y Laura Davies”. Las dos estaban colgadas en forma de póster en la habitación de Paula durante su etapa universitaria. Bingo. Sería Davies una vez más quien tomó el testigo y trabajó la estrategia con la catalana: empezaría Davies porque salían en el primer partido abriendo la Solheim Cup del 2002. Todo iba según lo previsto... hasta que llegaron al tee del 1. "Me dijo: «Oye... que estoy muy nerviosa. Sales tú primero». Paula todavía se ríe al recordarlo. "Yo esperaba acompañar a Laura... no pegar el primer golpe de la Solheim”. Aquella vuelta dejó otra escena inolvidable, en el hoyo 18 Laura pegó un drive de los suyos y Paula decidió arriesgar con una madera 3 espectacular. Laura Davies le dijo entre risas, "Me has quitado todo el protagonismo”. Y unos hoyos antes, cuando Paula, manojo de nervios, le pisó la línea del putt, ella respondió, "Ya ves... para lo que pesas”. Así era Laura, humor británico en estado puro. "Aquella Solheim fue un antes y un después. Crecí como jugadora, como persona y como atleta, y hasta encontré a mi representante”. Y así son muchas Solheim. La Solheim de 2003 fue histórica para Ana Belén Sánchez. Y para la propia Solheim Cup pues era la primera vez que salía de las Islas Británicas para disputarse en Suecia. Pero fue histórica para la malagueña no solo porque ganaron, sino porque era la primera vez que sus padres viajaban para verla competir. "Había que verles... No sé cómo pudo aguantar los nervios mi padre." Ella tampoco estaba mucho más tranquila. "Todo el rato pensaba: ¿qué hago yo aquí, con este pedazo de jugadoras?" hasta que estrellas como Annika Sorenstam le llamaban por su nombre y empezó a disfrutar. "Más presión que la Solheim es imposible tener. Después de aquello empecé a jugar con muchísima más confianza." Pasaron seis años hasta volver a ver una española en la Solheim, y sin victoria europea, todo hay que decirlo, y fue la donostiarra Tania Elósegui en Illinois en 2009. Antes incluso de pegar un golpe recibió un mensaje. Era de José María Olazábal. "Me dijo: 'Pase lo que pase, disfruta de cada momento y todo lo que puedas y no te dejes intimidar en el tee del 1”, algo difícil pero el consejo funcionó. "No hay nada que se parezca a la Solheim. Compartir equipo con las jugadoras que habían marcado una época, Laura Davies, Suzann Petersen o Catriona Matthew era impresionante." Aunque quizás de los momentos más gratificantes fue en el hoyo 16 de los individuales, cuando metió un putt crucial y se encontró a compatriotas como Alex Armas celebrando como la que más. Si alguien conoce el alma del vestuario europeo es Azahara Muñoz. Se estrenó en el año 2011 en Irlanda, “yo era muy jovencita, y nos emparejaron a la más joven con la más mayor, a Catriona y a mi. La primera siempre es la que más te marca, porque vives momentos, situaciones y sensaciones absolutamente nuevas y espectaculares”. La Solheim es emoción, es pasión y son risas, porque los mejores recuerdos no se quedan en los campos de golf, sino en los vestuarios, en las salas de prensa o en el autobús. “Volvíamos al hotel cantando. Había una canción a la que cambiábamos la letra y le poníamos los nombres de las americanas. Se convirtió en la canción de cada Solheim." Y las bromas seguían en las ruedas de prensa. "Elegíamos un cantante y teníamos que meter letra de sus canciones en las respuestas que les dábamos a los periodistas. A veces no venían ni a cuento, pero nos moríamos de risa”. Eso nunca aparece en televisión, pero explica mejor que cualquier estadística por qué el equipo europeo es tan difícil de derrotar. Luego llegaban los momentos históricos, como el medio punto decisivo en esa misma edición de Killeen Castle, "Fue muy especial”. O lograr silenciar al público americano en Colorado. "Jugamos tan bien que el público americano se quedó completamente callado”. O la remontada de Gleneagles, "Con el putt de Suzann Pettersen aquello fue un éxtasis”. Y entre todos esos recuerdos, uno muy personal. "Jugar con Carlota en parejas en Colorado y ganar en el 18 haciendo birdie fue una auténtica locura. He tenido la suerte de ganar tres Solheim y compartirlo con el equipo es algo demasiado especial." Porque el año 2013 fue sonado, era la primera vez que las europeas ganaban en suelo americano y de las 12 jugadoras que componen el equipo de la Solheim Cup, tres eran españolas: Azahara Muñoz, con una Solheim a sus espaldas, hacía de cicerone a Carlota Ciganda y Beatriz Recari, que se estrenaban con éxito aplastante en Colorado, confirmando el extraordinario momento que vivía aquella generación española. La navarra Beatriz Recari se había quedado a las puertas del equipo en dos ocasiones, pero Colorado fue la definitiva para dejar su huella. “Jugar la Solheim era mi meta y gracias a Dios pude vivirla; la recuerdo con muchísimo cariño, emoción, fue una semana irrepetible, es muy difícil explicar lo que se vive allí, es una presión muy interesante de vivir. Cada semana pierdes o ganas tú, pero esa semana representas a Europa, a todo un continente, que son palabras mayores. Sentimientos, sensaciones, el vestuario, todo es bonito. Eso sí, antes de ir al tee del 1 es mejor no tomar café, porque es un test de Parkinson bastante fuerte”. Y llegamos a Carlota Ciganda, que jugará esta semana, con 36 años, su octava Solheim consecutiva. A día de hoy no se entiende esta competición sin ella, y sigue hablando de ella como una niña que espera el día de Reyes. "Lo que más me gusta es el ambiente de equipo, estar ahí para ayudar, jugar para algo más grande que tú: Europa, la capitana y tus compañeras. Eso me encanta." Carlota tiene muchos recuerdos maravillosos de su competición favorita, esos partidos con Azahara que tanto nos han recordado a la pareja Seve-Chema en la Ryder Cup. Pero si tiene que recordar uno, tiene grabado para siempre aquel hierro al 17 frente a Nelly Korda en Finca Cortesín, "Son momentos que no se olvidan”.Probablemente porque toda España lo celebró con ella casi como cuando ganamos el mundial. Esta semana Julia López, 23 años, descubrirá todo esto por primera vez. Recibirá consejos, escuchará historias y seguirá escribiendo la suya. Raquel Carriedo, la pionera le recomienda tranquilidad, "Que disfrute, aunque suene a tópico. Va a salir curtida y lo va a notar”. Y Carlota solo piensa en ayudarla, "Quiero que todo el mundo vea lo buenísima jugadora que es”. Porque esa es otra tradición de la Solheim, las veteranas reciben a las nuevas igual que un día Davies recibió a Carriedo o Martí. Y dentro de unos años, cuando Julia recuerde su primera Solheim, probablemente tampoco hablará solo de golf. Hablará del primer tee, de los nervios, del vestuario, de las risas, de las canciones y de esas pequeñas historias que nunca aparecen en el leadeboard. Porque la Solheim se disputa durante tres días, pero deja recuerdos para toda la vida. Quizá por eso la Solheim nunca se explica del todo con los resultados. Se explica con un autobús lleno de jugadoras cantando, con una capitana que te abraza cuando más lo necesitas, con una leyenda como Laura Davies confesando que también tiene nervios antes del primer golpe o con una broma en una rueda de prensa que solo entiende el vestuario. Esos pequeños momentos son los que convierten una competición en algo mucho más grande. Y son los que hacen que, veinte años después, las veteranas españolas sigan hablando de la Solheim con la misma ilusión que la primera vez. Eso es lo que hace diferente a la Solheim Cup.

articles.title: $37.4M worth of leftovers? Or keys to Cowboys’ defensive turnaround?
articles.summary: The Cowboys are hoping to get more out of Kenny Clark and Rashon Gary than what the Packers were.
articles.body:
The Dallas Cowboys took a different approach to roster building over the last two years. Instead of bargain hunting leftovers, or gambling on busts, they acted more calculated, hunting the under-appreciated. From George Pickens and Javonte Williams to Jonathan Bullard and Otito Ogbonnia , the Cowboys have been searching for specific types of players who they think will thrive in Dallas.

They say, "one man's trash is another man's treasure," and that especially rings true for a pair of former Green Bay Packers . Rashan Gary , OLB, and Kenny Clark , DT, are two players the Cowboys picked up from the Packers via trades over the last 13 months.

Clark, a former Pro Bowl tackle, was included in the Micah Parsons trade last summer. He was a piece the Cowboys insisted upon and a player who makes the defensive system work. Green Bay fans and media were quick to discredit the player, citing his decline in play and his tenuousness on the future roster.

Gary, picked up roughly six months later, was another player who had fallen out of favor in Green Bay. But instead of being called a "has been" he was dubbed a "never was" by the Packer faithful. As a former first-round pick, Gary never quite lit the world on fire like he was supposed to, so he was said to be another player who was likely to be cut.

The Cowboys clearly see both players differently. Not only are both starters for the Cowboys in 2026, but Clark has been voted team captain as an anchor of the defense. Dallas doesn't expect either player to suddenly vault up to Pro Bowl levels, but they do consider each to be valuable up-cycles.

Clark, working on a contract that averages $21,333,333 in APY, and Gary, working on a $16M APY deal, aren't cheap players, which might explain some of the saltiness from the people who consider cheese a major food group and a blaze-orange vest proper church attire. But in Dallas, their contracts carry much more palatable cap hits this season, combining for $15,200,000 in 2026.

Clark and Gary have contracts that will cost Dallas beyond the 2026 season whether they return next year or not. That makes them players who are critical to the present and future of the team. The question that remains is whether the Cowboys can get more out of them than the Packers thought they were capable, or if they made a mistake trading for expensive castoffs Green Bay was already done with.

articles.body:
Team USA arrive in the Netherlands as defending champions and look to claim their first victory on European soil since 2015, two years on from their 15.5-12.5 home victory in Virginia.

Angela Stanford has world No 1 Nelly Korda among a strong line-up that contains 10 players with past Solheim Cup experience, with Team USA looking to overcome recent near-misses in away editions.

English duo Charley Hull and Lottie Woad headline Anna Nordqvist's European side, which contains six members of the team that salvaged a dramatic 14-14 tie in the 2023 edition on home soil.

Each of the last four Solheim Cups on European soil - along with the 2021 edition in America - have seen the teams separated by two points or less, with few reasons to suggest why this week's contest will be any different.

Who do the Sky Sports and Golf Channel pundits think will win the 2026 Solheim Cup? Who could be the star of the European team and which players could be ones to have key roles? We asked them for their predictions…

Team USA are chasing back-to-back wins for the first time since 2017, with Alison Lee the only player in their side that feature in their dramatic 14.5-13.5 comeback win in Germany two years earlier.

Home teams historically have the edge in the Solheim Cup, with five of Europe's seven wins in this event - including a 15-13 success in Ireland 2011 and a dramatic 14.5-13.5 win at Gleneagles in 2019 - coming at home.

"This is more of a European golf course than the one in Spain, which will maybe lean towards the Europeans," Sky Sports' Sophie Walker said. "But it looks a little bit like a Walton Heath to me and the Americans did all right there at the AIG Women's Open!"

Both two previous occasions that a captain has named three rookies among their picks, that side has gone on to win.

Team Europe did it 2011 and 2021, with the hosts now looking to continue that streak as Nastasia Nadaud, Julia Lopez Ramirez and Mimi Rhodes join Woad in making their debuts.

articles.title: Solheim Cup 2026: Charley Hull to face Nelly Korda in opening foursomes match
articles.summary: Charley Hull and Lottie Woad will face the formidable pairing of Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz in Friday's opening match of the Solheim Cup in the Netherlands.
articles.body:
Europe's Charley Hull and Lottie Woad will face the formidable pairing of Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz in Friday's opening match of the Solheim Cup in the Netherlands.

While English pair Woad and Hull are seventh and eighth in the rankings, the American duo have won all four of their foursomes matches across the past two editions of the contest.

That included a victory over Hull and Esther Henseleit in the first match of the 2024 edition.

"Charley and Lottie, they've got to play [together] quite a bit on tour this year, so I think they were both very excited to be paired with each other," said Europe's captain Anna Nordqvist.

"If you are going to be anywhere [on Friday morning] you want to be on the first tee because it doesn't get better than that."

US captain Angela Stanford, added: "If I didn't put those two out [Korda and Corpuz], I would be questioned. I feel like the whole world knew that they were coming.

"We can talk about Nelly and we can talk about her being the number one player in the world, but don't sleep on Allisen. I've called her the backbone of our team.

"She's pretty tough. There are a lot of good things going on in that pairing that, you know, they just complement each other really well."

Play gets under way at Bernardus Golf at 06:40 BST with four foursomes (alternate shot) matches.

Denmark's Nanna Koerstz Madsen is paired with France's Celine Boutier in match two and they take on Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin.

Germany's Henseleit and Ireland's Leona Maguire will play Andrea Lee and debutant Lindy Duncan, while Swedish duo Maja Stark and Linn Grant get started against Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho.

The United States have dominated the previous two opening foursomes sessions, winning 4-0 at Finca Cortesin in 2023 and taking a 3-1 advantage at the Robert Trent Jones Golf Club in 2024.

Europe are looking to regain the trophy after losing 15½-12½ in Virginia two years ago in the biggest team competition in women's golf.

articles.title: Councillor vows to lie naked in mud over carbon capture pipeline
articles.summary: Councillor Kathy Hodson makes the plea before a debate on running carbon capture pipes on council land.
articles.body:
A councillor has offered to "lay in the mud naked" in order to prevent a carbon capture pipeline being built.

Wirral Councillors unanimously voted on Wednesday against granting developers access to council land for a major gas pipe project, Peak Cluster, that could cut through the full length of the borough.

Councillors were told before the debate if they had already made their decision and did not have an open mind they should not take part in the vote.

Reform UK's Kathy Hodson told the meeting she therefore would not vote because she "would be voting against it no matter what", adding that she was willing to "lay in the mud naked" to prevent the land being dug up.

Peak Cluster is a £5bn carbon capture project backed by the government.

The proposed underground pipe would take carbon dioxide from lime and cement manufacturing sites in Derbyshire and Staffordshire and transport them to be stored off-shore under the Irish Sea with the pipe traversing the length of the Wirral Peninsular before heading into the sea.

Peak Cluster has previously said it would work with experts to minimise the environmental impact of the pipeline and when operational, the project would prevent three million tonnes of carbon dioxide going into the atmosphere every year.

Wirral Council's Policy and Resource committee heard there was a request to grant land access to Peak Cluster to carry out a number of surveys.

A report to the committee explained that following refusal: "Peak Cluster will be in a position to authorise staff and contractors to access the land and if the council were to in any way impede access, then Peak Cluster would be entitled to seek a warrant from a magistrates court."

The rest of the committee, who did take part in the vote, unanimously rejected Peak Cluster's request.

There was cross-party consensus at Wallasey Town Hall, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

Labour Party councillor, Mark Skillicorn, said that ever since the papers for the meeting were released, there had been a lot of anxiety among residents.

Lib Dem, Green, and Conservative councillors also all opposed the request and project in general.

Coucillor Paula Basnett, leader of the council's Labour group who chaired the meeting, thanked residents for sending their views.

Green councillor Gail Jenkinson said after the vote: "Sadly, Peak Cluster is still likely to be able to proceed with them relatively quickly through other legal powers but our opposition remains resolute.

"We do not support this pipeline or the construction of a huge Above Ground Installation here.

"We will continue the fight to protect Wirral, its residents and its environment."

Once built, the Peak Cluster underground pipeline would transport harmful carbon dioxide emissions from Derbyshire to the Wirral Coastline

From here, the gas would be compressed and stored within a former gas reservoir deep under the Irish Sea, off the coast of Morecambe in Lancashire, where the emissions would not be able to do any damage to the environment

articles.title: Solheim Cup 2026: Charley Hull and Lottie Woad to face Team USA star Nelly Korda as Friday foursomes line-up revealed
articles.summary: Charley Hull and Lottie Woad to face unbeaten foursomes pair Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz on Friday morning at Bernardus Golf; Team USA have won the opening session the previous two Solheim Cups; watch day one live on Friday from 6am on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
The world No 8 makes her eighth consecutive appearance for Team Europe and will lead out the hosts at Bernardus Golf alongside compatriot Lottie Woad, one of four rookies in Anna Nordqvist's team, with the English duo facing unbeaten Korda and Allisen Corpuz in the Friday foursomes.

Korda and Corpuz have won all four foursomes matches together over the last two Solheim Cups and look to extend that perfect record when they tee off at 7.40am local time (6.40am BST), as Team USA begin their bid to retain the trophy and claim a first victory on European soil since 2015.

Alison Lee - the only player involved from that American away win in Germany - partners Lauren Coughlin, with the pair facing Team Europe stalwart Celine Boutier and Denmark's returning Nanna Koerstz Madsen in the second match of the morning.

Esther Henseleit has been paired with Leona Maguire, having been paired with Hull in foursomes during her previous Solheim Cup appearance in 2024, with the pair taking on Andrea Lee and rookie Lindy Duncan, while Swedish duo Maja Stark and Linn Grant go up against Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho.

Friday's foursomes line-up (all times BST)

0640 Charley Hull and Lottie Woad vs Allisen Corpuz and Nelly Korda

0652 Nanna Koerstz Madsen and Celine Boutier vs Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin

0704 Esther Henseleit and Leona Maguire vs Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan

0716 Maja Stark and Linn Grant vs Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho

Hull key for Team Europe in bid for fast start?

Woad is the only debutant sent out by Nordqvist on the opening morning, with Team Europe looking for a faster start than they've managed in the first session of the last two Solheim Cups.

Team USA swept the opening session of the historic 14-14 tie in 2023 and built a 3-1 advantage on their way to home victory the following year, having previously failed to lead after the first morning of the previous six Solheim Cups.

"They [Korda and Corpuz] have a nice rapport about them, so I felt like they earned the right to go out first," Team USA captain Angela Stanford said. "I feel like if I didn't put those two out, I would be questioned! The whole world knew they were coming."

Hull top-scored for Europe in their 2024 loss and despatched Korda 6&4 in their Sunday singles clash, with the 30-year-old likely to play a key role in home hopes this week and always a likely playing partner for Woad.

"I feel like over the years that the Solheim Cup has really grown on her [Hull]," Nordqvist said. "She has been buzzing and so excited since she got here on Monday. Her and Lottie have got to play quite a bit on the LPGA Tour this year, so I think they were very excited to be here with each other."

Rookies Mimi Rhodes, Nastasia Nadaud and Julia Lopez Ramirez all sit out of the opening session for Team Europe, along with Carlota Ciganda in her eighth consecutive appearance.

Angel Yin has also been left out of the morning session but confirmed as available to feature later in the event, with the two-time LPGA Tour winner previously a fitness doubt after only completing one 72-hole event since May.

Debutant Auston Kim, Megan Khang and Yealimi Noh are the others to be benched for the opening session, while the captain's agreement in place means every player has to play at least once over the first two days.

Foursomes sees two golfers from Europe compete against a pair from the USA, with team members alternating between shots and each team using one ball. Each match is worth one point, with Team USA requiring 14 points this week to retain the trophy and either team needing 14.5 points for victory.

Sky Sports Golf will have at least 12 hours of live coverage from the first two days, with coverage getting under way at 6am on Friday and Saturday ahead of the opening foursomes match teeing off at 6.40am (7.40am local time).

The afternoon fourballs are scheduled to start at 12.05pm (1.05pm local time) on both days, with coverage continuing until after the final putt is holed, while Sunday singles coverage begins at 9am ahead of the opening tee shot at 10.10am.

articles.title: Projecting Baltimore’s edge-rusher rotation
articles.summary: Baltimore has five edge defenders capable of production and impact behindTrey Hendrickson
articles.body:
After months of waiting, the Ravens will debut a retooled, swagger-filled defense with plenty of playmakers and a closer at the edge rusher spot. Trey Hendrickson will lead Baltimore's pass rush, but the Ravens have several options for constructing the rotation around him.

Hendrickson should play the majority of high-leverage passing downs and could approach 70% of the defensive snaps.

Tavius Robinson is the likely early-down starter opposite him because of his size and ability to set the edge. Mike Green should replace Robinson in obvious passing situations and could finish games with the second-highest snap total in the group. First-round pick Zion Young has the power and frame to contribute against the run before expanding his pass-rush role. His early development should earn him a place in the weekly rotation.

Undrafted rookie Ethan Burke forced his way onto the roster with consistent preseason pressure. His 6-foot-6 frame makes him an intriguing situational option, though special teams will determine how often he dresses and how often he is inactive. Kyle Hamilton and Roquan Smith can also blitz, while Calais Campbell can rush from the edge in heavier fronts.

articles.title: Brooks Koepka confirms the real reason why he agreed to join TGL
articles.summary: Brooks Koepka will be joining TGL in 2027 as part of the brand new Motor City Golf Club team. Koepka left the PGA Tour in order to join LIV Golf in June 2022...
articles.body:
Brooks Koepka will be joining TGL in 2027 as part of the brand new Motor City Golf Club team.

Koepka left the PGA Tour in order to join LIV Golf in June 2022.

However, the 36-year-old American decided to leave LIV at the end of 2025, and he made his PGA Tour return just a few weeks later.

Brooks Koepka actually struggled on the PGA Tour in 2026, managing to record just one top-10 finish all season long.

Koepka described his 2026 season as 'pathetic' , and he will be hopeful of big improvements in 2027.

And the five-time major winner has decided to link up with TGL in 2027 in order to help give him something extra.

Brooks Koepka confirms the real reason why he agreed to join TGL

Koepka spoke to The Mirror ahead of the Irish Open this week at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg.

He was asked why he decided to join TGL ahead of the new 2027 season.

" I felt comfortable when I met with TGL, " Koepka admitted.

" It's something to do. It's close by, and I think if you kind of look at it, the guys who have played well over the last little bit have played in it.

" I don't know if there's an advantage to it or not. But it seems like something fun, something I'm interested in. I think it will be a cool experience. "

Brooks Koepka comments on putting his old putter back in the bag

Koepka has his old putter back in the bag at the Irish Open this week – the one that helped him win five major championships.

" You can't really get a feel for it until the competition. But, everything feels like it's going in the right direction, " he said.

" I'm just trying to stay positive. I still believe I can go win any week, any day, any tournament. But when you're putting like that and it's holding you back, it's very tough to win.

" You've just got to deal with it and move on and make some changes. "

If Koepka putts well this week at the Irish Open, he will almost certainly contend to win, such is the quality of his ball-striking.

articles.title: Nobody wants AI-generated sports commentators, but a pro golf tournament is introducing one anyway
articles.summary: The New Mexico Open will debut Duff Foreman, an AI-generated golf commentator joining Notah Begay III on a live YouTube broadcast this week.
articles.body: Golf fans who tune into this week's New Mexico Open broadcast will be introduced to a new commentator by the name of Duff Foreman. He'll join former PGA Tour winner Notah Begay III and well-known broadcaster Ryan Burr on the call, although Foreman won't technically be on site, seeing as how he's not an actual person. Foreman is believed to be the first-ever AI-generated golf commentator that will be interacting live on-screen alongside human hosts. It is expected that Foreman will jump into unscripted conversations while providing insights and commentary about the play, the golf course, weather, conditions, and the rules of the game throughout nine hours of live coverage. The very obvious question here is why? Why are we (humans) adding an AI character (not a human) to a golf broadcast? The New Mexico Open may only be a state tournament streamed on YouTube and televised locally, but it is still a professional event with a purse of $137,000 being contested by Sun Country PGA, a section of the PGA of America. OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD Begay, who will be pulling double duty and teeing it up in the tournament, tried to justify why an AI character is joining the broadcast. "Golf fans are always looking for a better understanding of what players are thinking and why they make certain decisions," Begay said in a press release shared by tournament organizers. "If Duff Foreman delivers what we’re expecting, he’ll become another voice in the broadcast, helping us explain strategy, analyze swings, consider changing conditions like weather and course setup, and answer questions in real time. I think that kind of conversation could make the game more interesting and enjoyable for viewers." Begay is right, golf fans are constantly looking for more insights involving the game and how players go about their business during competition. However, his claim that an AI-generated character that was built on a computer is going to deliver a better understanding of what a human is thinking and how said human comes to a decision may be one of the most disingenuous comments ever shared in an official press release, and in the year 2026, that is saying something. The "conversation" Begay is hopeful to have with the AI commentator will not be "enjoyable for viewers;" it will be universally hated and mocked, just like the rollout of Foreman across social media in the buildup to the event has been. Foreman has an X account that not only posts nothing but pointless AI slop, but also has a link in the bio section that directs viewers to a YouTube channel called X-Treme Golf. There, you'll find more AI content, such as Foreman playing golf from the summit of Mt. Everest. Foreman and this 'content' are largely seen as being pointless and disturbingly dystopian from a public point of view, which brings us back to the original question: Why is an AI-generated commentator being added to a golf broadcast? For starters, those behind the scenes of the Foreman launch who are welcoming his character to the broadcast are seeing the situation differently. "That’s the interesting thing about social media, it gives everyone an opportunity to voice their opinions. There are critics for pretty much everything related to new technologies, especially something that is as impactful, informational, and entertaining as Duff," Cory Armstrong, executive director of Sun Country Golf House, shared. "There have been about 250 million media impressions about Duff since July 14 on television, radio, print, online, and on social media. Our research from third party media tracking platforms is showing 96% positive sentiment. Negative sentiment is about 1%. So, Duff is still doing quite well in terms of acceptance. We certainly hope people will receive our championship and the streaming broadcast positively. By using Duff as a tool to gain attention and provide information, more people will learn about the history of the New Mexico Open, the quality of its players, the challenge of the course, the mission and programs of our organizations, and the businesses of our corporate partners." Positive ratings paint one answer from one perspective, but I think there is another answer to the ‘why’ of it all, and it is both wildly complicated and extremely straightforward. We're living in incredibly bizarre times where everything you look at, it seems AI is grabbing hold of whatever that something is. Whether the impact of AI is having a positive or negative impact varies depending on the situation and the humans being impacted, but AI is here, and it is evolving by the day. This brings us to the straightforwardness of it all. You – and that 'you' includes golf broadcasts now – can not afford to be the last one to peek around the corner to see what that something is when everyone seems to be fighting to have the first glimpse. articles.title: Niemann manda, Cabrera Bello responde y Rahm resiste al viento
articles.standfirst: Condiciones de juego exigentes en la primera ronda del Amgen Irish Open del DP World Tour
articles.summary: Condiciones de juego exigentes en la primera ronda del Amgen Irish Open del DP World Tour
articles.body: El Amgen Irish Open descubrió este jueves la cara más auténtica y también más despiadada de Doonbeg. El viento fue ganando protagonismo con el paso de las horas, el ritmo de juego se hizo desesperadamente lento y la primera jornada terminó suspendida por falta de luz con varios partidos todavía en el campo. En ese escenario, Joaquin Niemann (-5) dejó la referencia con una magnífica tarjeta de 65 golpes, Rafa Cabrera Bello (-2) firmó la mejor vuelta española y Jon Rahm (PAR) consiguió mantenerse en pie en una tarde en la que cada par terminó teniendo un enorme valor. Niemann aprovechó las mejores condiciones de la primera parte del día para establecer en 65 golpes el nuevo récord del campo con la configuración preparada para este Irish Open. El chileno dejó el listón en cinco bajo par y terminó la jornada con dos golpes de ventaja sobre Shaun Norris (-3) y Shane Lowry (-3), aunque su liderato no es todavía definitivo. Adrian Meronk (-3), después de 15 hoyos, Maximilian Steinlechner (-3), tras 13, y Renato Paratore (-3), después de 12, estaban entre los jugadores que todavía podían darle caza cuando la falta de luz obligó a detener el juego. El viento convirtió el estreno de Doonbeg como sede del torneo en una prueba de golf y, sobre todo, de paciencia. El ritmo llegó a ser tedioso. El partido estelar de Rahm, Lowry y Reed necesitó cerca de tres horas para completar apenas siete hoyos y, a medida que avanzó la tarde, los gestos de desesperación se multiplicaron. El campo parecía otro respecto al que se habían encontrado los primeros partidos. En esas condiciones, la vuelta de Rafa Cabrera Bello adquirió todavía más mérito. El grancanario llegó al tee del 16 con cuatro bajo par, segundo en solitario, después de firmar birdies en los hoyos 3, 4, 10 y 12 y recorrer los primeros 15 sin cometer un solo bogey. El viento terminó cobrándose su peaje. Bogey en el par 3 del 16 y otro en el exigente 18 para un 68 que dejó un pequeño sabor agridulce por lo que pudo haber sido, pero que sin ningún género de dudas, por las condiciones de juego, supone un magnífico comienzo y le sitúa a tres golpes del líder. También tuvo que fajarse de lo lindo Jon Rahm (PAR). El de Barrika comenzó con un birdie en el 2 embocando desde unos cinco metros, pero perdió el golpe en el 5 después de fallar la calle por la derecha. En el par cinco del 8 dispuso de una magnífica oportunidad después de dos grandes golpes y un alivio sin penalidad por un aspersor, pero dejó escapar un putt de aproximadamente metro y medio que tal vez podía haberle ayudado a empezar a lanzar su ronda. Su paso por las segunda mitad de Doonbeg fue un continuo tira y afloja. Birdie en el par cinco del 10, bogey en el 11 y nueva reacción inmediata con birdie en el 12. En el 13 llegó uno de los pares más valiosos de su tarjeta: mandó su golpe de salida tan a la derecha que jugó una provisional ante la posibilidad de no encontrar la primera, pero apareció y desde allí fabricó una gran recuperación para salvar el par. Uno de esos que se celebran tanto o más que un birdie. Doonbeg volvió a cobrarle un golpe en el par tres del 14. Rahm no encontró el green desde el tee, su recuperación no fue suficientemente precisa y falló el putt de par. Regresaba así al resultado de par y desde ahí ya no cedió: cuatro pares consecutivos del 15 al 18 para 70 golpes, cinco más que Niemann. No fue la vuelta que buscaba el golfista vasco en su regreso al DP World Tour una vez finalizada la temporada de LIV Golf, pero tampoco una tarjeta que le deje fuera de nada. Y mucho menos después de comprobar cómo se comportó el campo durante la tarde. Un ejemplo extremo fue Francesco Molinari (+2): llegó a colocarse cuatro bajo par y terminó firmando 72 golpes, perdiendo seis golpes en el tramo final de su recorrido. Rahm persigue además esta semana un objetivo con un enorme componente histórico. Ya ganó el Irish Open en Portstewart en 2017 y en Lahinch en 2019, por lo que una victoria el domingo sería la tercera de su carrera y le permitiría igualar los tres títulos de Seve Ballesteros, campeón en 1983, 1985 y 1986. Todo ello en un torneo que por primera vez visita Doonbeg y se disputa en el complejo propiedad de Donald Trump, con la posibilidad todavía por confirmar de que el presidente estadounidense pueda estar presente el domingo y participar en la entrega del trofeo. Entre golpe y golpe hubo incluso tiempo para descubrir una faceta menos conocida del golfista de Barrika. Rahm contó que practicó taekwondo de niño por su afición a las artes marciales y que incluso volvió a practicarlo cuando ya era profesional, animado por su fisioterapeuta, hasta alcanzar el cinturón amarillo. "Eso fue hace mucho tiempo. Me gustan las artes marciales y me ha gustado practicarlas", explicó. La llegada de los hijos terminó por quitarle el tiempo necesario para continuar, aunque reconoció que sigue siendo "fan" y un apasionado de esta disciplina. Entre las grandes estrellas, el defensor del título, Rory McIlroy (-1), también comprobó lo caro que podía resultar un error. Arrancó de maravilla con birdies en el 2 y el 4 y conservó el dos bajo par en el acumulado hasta el hoyo 13, donde un doble bogey borró de una tacada todo el trabajo anterior. No hizo ningún bogey en toda la jornada y reaccionó con un birdie en el 15 para entregar un 69 que le mantiene a cuatro golpes de Niemann. Un golpe mejor terminó Patrick Reed (-2). El estadounidense entregó un 68 que cobra especial importancia en su pelea por la Race to Dubai, de la que es líder con 2.990,12 puntos, por delante precisamente de McIlroy. Reed continúa así sumando argumentos en una temporada europea extraordinariamente regular y se coloca a sólo tres golpes de la cabeza. Por detrás de Cabrera Bello y Rahm, Alejandro del Rey (PAR) completó también una sólida primera jornada con 70 golpes. Jorge Campillo (+1) y David Puig (+1) entregaron sendos 71, mientras Pablo Larrazábal (+1) fue uno de los españoles afectados por la suspensión y tendrá que completar su vuelta después de quedarse en el hoyo 14. Más atrás terminaron Eugenio Chacarra (+2) y Nacho Elvira (+2), ambos con 72, y Ángel Ayora (+3), con 73. Chacarra, tercero actualmente en la Race to Dubai, tendrá que recuperar terreno este viernes para no comprometer su presencia durante el fin de semana. La parte más amarga de la nutrida representación española correspondió a Ángel Hidalgo (+5), Manuel Elvira (+5) y Sergio García (+5), todos con 75 golpes. Sergio terminó además igualado con Brooks Koepka, otra de las grandes figuras que sufrió ante Doonbeg. Adrián Otaegui (+6) entregó un 76 e Iván Cantero (+8) cerró con 78. La clasificación completa, en cualquier caso, tendrá que esperar. La combinación del viento, la dificultad de un links que fue endureciéndose conforme avanzó el día y un ritmo de juego extraordinariamente lento impidió completar la jornada antes de que la luz desapareciera en la costa oeste irlandesa. articles.title: Irish Open: Rory McIlroy four behind leader Joaquin Niemann after 'longest round' at Irish Open
articles.summary: Defending champion Rory McIlroy says his opening round at the Irish Open, which was played in stormy conditions and took in excess of six hours, may have been the longest of his career as he sits four behind leader Joacquin Niemann.
articles.body:
5 J Niemann (Chile); -3 S Lowry (Ire), S Norris (SA), A Meronk (Pol, 15*), M Steinlechner (Austria, 13*), R Paratore (Ita, 12*); -2 K Kobori, (NZ), R Cabrera (Spa), T McKibbin (NI), P Reed (US), C Syme (Sco), N Noergaard (Den), F Lacroix (Fra), J Skov Olesen (Den, 17*), R Langasque (Fra, 16*), D Law (Sco, 12*)

Selected others: -1 E Ferguson (Sco), A Sullivan (Eng), N Hoejgaard (Den), R McIlroy (NI); Level J Rahm (Spa); +1 P Harrington (Ire); +2 R MacIntyre (Sco); +3 L Donald (Eng); +5 S Garcia (Spa), B Koepka (US); +8 T Hatton (Eng)

* denotes number of holes played in uncompleted rounds

Rory McIlroy said his first round at the Irish Open at Doonbeg on Thursday may have been the longest of his career as he ended a wind-ravaged day one sitting four shots behind leader Joaquin Niemann.

McIlroy's opening one-under-par 69 took in excess of six hours as he and the rest of the field battled the high winds and sporadic showers which battered the Trump International Golf Links in County Clare.

The world number two posted birdies at the second and fourth holes, double-bogeyed the 13th after taking two shots to get out of a bunker, but then picked up a shot at the 15th.

Back-to-back Masters champion McIlroy is aiming to defend the title he won at the K Club last year and secure a third Irish Open crown of his career, having triumphed at the same venue in 2016.

Victory this week would mean he draws level with European greats Seve Ballesteros, Nick Faldo, Bernhard Langer and Colin Montgomerie on three Irish Open successes.

"I can't recall a round of golf that has taken that long before. We've had some rounds that have taken five and a half hours or maybe five and three quarters, but over six hours might be a first for me," McIlroy told BBC Sport NI.

"It was tough conditions, very windy, it was hard to get into any sort of rhythm out there. It was kind of stop-start, so I felt like shooting under par wasn't exactly what I wanted, but at the end of the day I'm only four shots behind and not in a bad spot going into the next three days.

"It was tough, but you kind of just got the hang of it, you just kept the ball as close to the ground as possible and just made as many pars as you could.

"You were hitting into the wind on average three or four clubs more than you usually would. I had 138 yards to the last green there and hit my full seven iron. I usually hit my seven iron in warm, dry conditions 190 yards."

A run of four consecutive birdies between the 14th and 17th helped Chilean Niemann assume his position at the top of the leaderboard.

The LIV golfer had six birdies in total, with just a single dropped shot, to hold a two-shot lead over a group of five players, including Ireland's Shane Lowry and South African Shaun Norris, who both completed their first rounds.

Italian Renato Paratore, Maximilian Steinlechner of Austria, and Pole Adrian Meronk are also on three under but are among a number of players who must return to finish their opening 18 holes on Friday morning after fading light brought a halt to proceedings on Thursday evening.

Play was slow throughout the day as the inclement weather posed significant challenges for later starters in particular.

Northern Ireland's Tom McKibbin, who was three under for his first four holes, Scot Conor Syme and Race to Dubai leader Patrick Reed are among those on two under.

Two-time Irish Open champion Jon Rahm was left to rue an unproductive day on the greens as he shot a level-par 70.

Robert MacIntyre lies two over, with five-time major winner Brooks Koepka and Sergio Garcia three further back on five over, and European Ryder Cup player Tyrrell Hatton eight over.

Koepka's cause was not aided by a triple bogey at the first, quickly followed by a dropped shot at the second, and he will require an improved round on Friday if he is to avoid a second successive missed cut at the event.

articles.title: Packers Week 1 Preview: Why the Vikings are dangerous
articles.summary: There are few worse teams for the Packers and their young, banged-up line to face in a week 1 matchup.
articles.body:
The Minnesota Vikings went 9-8 last season despite the worst regular quarterback play I've ever seen. Something called Max Brosmer started a game against the Detroit Lions wherein he completed nine passes for 51 yards while taking seven sacks for 48 yards, and still somehow his team won the game.

The Vikings managed to pull off a winning record and finish ahead of the Lions via the head-to-head tiebreaker because their defensive coordinator Brian Flores is basically Tony Stark building the arc reactor in a cave in the desert with a box of scraps . He's unlike any other defensive coordinator in the league in that he almost never rushes the "normal" amount of people. It's always too many or too few, and it's never who you would expect. He's part necromancer, part general, part abstract painter. He's not thinking four moves ahead, he's performing moves in some other game he knows you will end up playing later but haven't even heard of yet. And for the Green Bay Packers , specifically, Brian Flores is going to be a problem on Sunday.

If the Packers were fully healthy, I wouldn't worry so much. If they had everyone going, I think they're familiar enough with the Flores attack that they would be able to work around it. I also think if they were playing the Bears, who have a terrible defense, or the Lions, who have a good-but-conventional defense, I would be picking the Packers to win this week. But as of Wednesday, Zack Bako-Bewele and Aaron Banks were limited in practice. I think Bako-Bewele probably plays, but there's a good chance he will be limited as he was much of last year, and if he can't go, the disaster that is Anthony Belton is likely to step in.

That's only a part of the problem though, as the interior of the Packers' line is easily their weakest unit, and their biggest vulnerability is with some combination of Sean Rhyan , Aaron Banks, Jacob Monk , and/or Jager Burton being charged with keeping the Flores blitzes at bay. Do you trust any of those guys to make the right read when Dallas Turner suddenly stunts inside, followed by Andrew Van Ginkel directly behind him while Jalen Redmond drops into coverage? Banks has been terrible in Green Bay , even when healthy, and there is no evidence he is healthy. The rest of them are, at best, "young and promising," but without experience against what Flores brings, this is very worrisome. They're even not very good when defenders are running right at them in predictable ways!

It's just a bad matchup, and it's made worse by the fact that Minnesota will likely be completely and totally unconcerned about the Packers' running game, with poor line play and no Josh Jacobs around. This will allow them to come after Jordan Love all day without much fear of getting burned. And since they coaxed Harrison Smith out of retirement to play safety, the Vikings will also have the benefit of a coach-on-the-field presence to help clean up any mistakes the younger Minnesota defenders make in the back end.

All of that said, the Vikings are not some juggernaut, and they have plenty of exploitable flaws in their own right. Gone are Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave (the latter headed to the Packers, where he too is limited in practice). Gone, most importantly, is Jonathan Greenard . The Vikings definitely lost some talent, and they definitely lack the experience necessary to run Flores' scheme perfectly. But their sack leaders from last season, (Dallas Turner, Andrew Van Ginkel, Eric Wilson , and Jalen Redmond) are all still on the team, and all perfectly capable of blitzing. Their leaders in passes defended (Van Ginkel, Harrison Smith, Byron Murphy , Josh Mettellus, and Isaiah Rodgers ) are all still on the team. There wasn't that much turnover. They've all played this system before.

Flores also seems to be the rare coordinator that is able to defy the highly variable nature of year-to-year defensive variance. One reason the Vikings are a popular pick to finish last in the division is that it's almost impossible to maintain defensive excellence for multiple seasons in a row. The Vikings have finished in the top three in FTN's DVOA metric for two consecutive seasons , and in the FTN Almanac author Dan Pizzuta points out that their projection system has the defense projected as about league average, but that if anyone can defy the odds, it might be Flores.

Over the course of the entire season I suspect the Vikings' defense is closer to tenth than first, as personnel absolutely matters. But for this game specifically? Andrew Van Ginkel is going to be abusing Monk/Belton/Banks over, and over, and over. Minnesota swept the Lions last year largely because Flores is so adept at finding the weak link on the other side of the field and exploiting it until you are forced to take that player off the field. Against the Lions, that was all-world running back Jahmyr Gibbs , who is amazing at everything but pass protection where he held a 50.5 pass blocking grade at PFF . Every time Gibbs was on the field, Flores overloaded the line and managed to get a blitzer singled up on him, resulting in five sacks of Jared Goff in each of their two games.

The Vikings had a 51.1% blitz rate last season, with the next-highest defense coming in at 39%. On early downs they blitzed even more at 54.7% of the time. If you can pick up the Vikings' blitz, you can almost certainly hurt them, and my hope for this game is that running back Chris Brooks , who is good in pass pro, and tight end Mark Redman see plenty of time to help out. But this matchup stinks for Green Bay, on the road, in a noisy indoor stadium, where Flores and Kevin O'Connell have had forever to prepare.

Worst of all, the Packers will not be able to fall back on terrible quarterback play with Kyler Murray now running the show. A quick reminder that this team went 13-4 just two seasons ago with a similar offensive unit (finishing 9th in points scored) and Sam Darnold at the helm before anyone thought Sam Darnold could be anything at all. Justin Jefferson finished that season with 1,533 yards and 10 touchdowns. I don't think Murray is great, but I don't think he has to be, and before Ben Johnson was the toast of the NFL as an offensive mind, Kevin O'Connell was right there in the conversation.

I am optimistic about the Packers overall. I think they are very talented up and down the roster (with a few small exceptions), and I even think they will get the line sorted eventually. Right now, however, other than facing an opponent like Seattle or Houston , this is as bad an opening matchup as they could have gotten given their current weaknesses and level of health.

articles.title: Packers news: Jordan Love protector gets injury update before Vikings game
articles.summary: After being a limited participant in practice on Wednesday, Green Bay Packers left tackle and Jordan Love protector Jordan Morgan appears to be ready to giv...
articles.body:
After being a limited participant in practice on Wednesday , Green Bay Packers left tackle and Jordan Love protector Jordan Morgan appears to be ready to give it a go for their upcoming Week 1 showdown against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday.

Morgan was listed as a full participant in Thursday's Green Bay practice, per the team's official injury report.

However, seven other Packers players either did not practice or were limited.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Nevertheless, Morgan's status update is a great sign for his availability in Green Bay's season opener, which will take place on the road, particularly at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis.

Green Bay still has one more practice on Friday before the Vikings clash, but that's normally just a walkthrough, which is why Morgan's full-participant status on Thursday is telling about his chances of being on the field for the Packers against Minnesota .

Morgan's knee issue was why he was previously limited in practice, but he appears healthy enough to see action.

"There's always concern when there's a guy on the injury report," Green Bay head coach Matt LaFleur said on Wednesday after Morgan's name showed up on the injury report as a limited participant (h/t Jason B. Hirschhorn of The Leap). "But as far as his availability, we're trying to build him up to get him in a spot where we feel like he's ready to go."

The 25-year-old Morgan is in his third NFL season. Green Bay welcomed him to the league as a first-round pick (25th overall) out of the Arizona Wildcats in the 2024 NFL Draft.
